title: Hermes Agent Consultant · Intermediate: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Where do fixed-duration gates like a security review belong in the estimate?
options: Hidden inside the build task they affect
Left out until the build is complete
Averaged into the total effort
On the critical path as their own items
questions.explanation: A gate runs on its owner's calendar and cannot be compressed by effort, so it must appear as a fixed-duration item on the critical path.

questions.question: An out-of-scope request arrives from one client. What is the right move?
options: Absorb the request quietly so that the client stays happy and never hears about it
Refuse the request bluntly and move on to the work already committed
Offer a re-scope conversation in the client's terms, with the trade and its cost
Delay the request so that the client eventually stops asking about it
questions.explanation: Out-of-scope work is a theft from another client's budget, so it needs a decision. Present it as the client's choice with real costs attached instead of refusing or absorbing silently.

questions.question: Why is a drive-by change to a live delivery a problem?
options: It is usually much larger than it looks and tends to break the whole build outright
Something now depends on the current behavior, and the change goes unrecorded
It costs considerably more compute to apply than a planned change would
It requires the client's legal team to review and sign a new agreement
questions.explanation: After handover the client's week is built around the current behavior, so a small unrecorded edit alters someone else's operation. A stream of them leaves nobody able to say what the system does.

questions.question: Why should at least two operators be trained to the same standard?
options: So the capability survives one of them leaving or changing roles
So the consultant can bill more hours to the engagement in total
So the two can divide the operational and change work between them
So the second operator can review the first operator's work before it runs
questions.explanation: A single trained person reintroduces the exact single point of failure the handover tried to remove. Two operators at the same standard keep the capability alive through any one absence.

questions.question: A live agent has failed while a client watches. What is the correct order of operations?
options: Patch first so that output resumes quickly, then diagnose and verify afterward
Verify first, then patch the change, then work out what actually caused it
Diagnose first, then patch, then verify the fix against a known-good result
Report to the client first, then patch, then diagnose if there is time
questions.explanation: A fix is a conclusion, not a first action. Patching on top of a wrong diagnosis entangles the failure, so you establish what is true before you change anything and verify after.

questions.question: What should set the length of each phase when a multi-week plan is built?
options: The time needed to reach its gate
A fixed allotment of weeks per phase
The consultant's weekly capacity
The order the phases are listed in
questions.explanation: Each phase ends at a gate, so its length is however long it takes to satisfy that gate, not a preassigned block of weeks.

questions.question: What must a seam between two owners contain to stay durable?
options: A verbal agreement that both owners renew each morning
What it delivers, needs, and its acceptance bar
The names of both owners and their roles
A status flag updated by the upstream owner
questions.explanation: A seam is an interface, and it stays usable only when both owners can read what the piece delivers, what it needs, and the bar it must meet.

questions.question: How should secrets be handled in a delivery?
options: Stored in environment variables or credential files, scoped to the task, kept out of prompts
Embedded directly in the scripts so that they are always available when the agent runs at night
Written into the operating doc so that the operator knows each value by heart
Shared across every agent in the estate to make rotation simpler for the team
questions.explanation: A credential belongs in an environment variable or credential file, scoped to the narrowest task that needs it. A leaking secret is the highest-severity, lowest-effort failure, so it is the first thing a reviewer checks.

questions.question: In the three-layer model of a discipline, which layer carries the transferable value?
options: The implementation layer, the exact syntax of the specific tool being ported
The intent layer, what the discipline is for and what bad outcome it prevents
The configuration layer, the specific set of files that the tool reads at startup
The vendor layer, the platform that the client has standardized on
questions.explanation: The intent survives any tool because it is what the discipline is for. Translation changes the implementation layer and leaves the intent and its mapping untouched.

questions.question: A failing gate is triaged as one of three diagnoses. Which set is correct?
options: A real regression, a stale reference, or a flaky test, each needing its own fix
A real regression, a capacity shortage, or a billing error, each needing its own fix
A blocked run, an expired key, or a delivery failure, each needing its own fix
A scope issue, a schedule issue, or a provider issue, each needing its own fix
questions.explanation: Naming the diagnosis is the whole skill because the fix differs: fix the system for a regression, update the case for stale reference, repair the test for a flaky gate.

questions.question: Why route mechanical work off the model and into a script?
options: A deterministic script costs nothing per run and cannot drift in judgment
A script produces genuinely higher-quality reasoning than a model on routine work
A script lets the whole fleet skip the need for any health signal at all
A script removes the need to model the weekly burn of the whole estate
questions.explanation: The cheapest reliable run is the one that never calls a model, and a deterministic check is the one component that cannot quietly change its own mind. Mechanical work gains nothing from reasoning.

questions.question: When a defect in the client's own data surfaces mid-build, what is the professional response?
options: Absorb the cleanup into the engagement because you are already working in the data
Quietly work around it without telling the client to avoid a difficult conversation
Name the defect with evidence, refuse to own it, and build a workaround
Pause the engagement entirely until the client fixes the data themselves
questions.explanation: Absorbing a pre-existing client defect costs unpaid days, teaches that exclusions are soft, and hides a governance problem. Naming it with evidence and pricing a workaround keeps ownership where it belongs.

questions.question: What distinguishes scope creep from normal, healthy addition to a project?
options: Creep is any addition the consultant personally finds tedious or unwelcome
Creep is addition outside the change process, so its cost is never visible
Creep is addition that makes the project run longer than a single calendar year
Creep is addition requested by a manager rather than by the sponsor
questions.explanation: Addition is normal; the problem is unmanaged addition whose cost never lands where the client can see it. The delta is only measurable against a written baseline.

questions.question: Which kind of number belongs in a report to the buyer?
options: The number of sessions and tokens the agent consumed over the period
The business effect the buyer would have paid for without the agent
The uptime percentage of the agent's runtime environment
The number of successful runs the scheduler completed this month
questions.explanation: Activity metrics describe the machinery and tell the buyer nothing they can act on. A number is worth reporting only when it maps to something the buyer would have paid for anyway.

questions.question: Under time-and-materials, what does the consultant owe the client in return for the client carrying the estimation risk?
options: A hard ceiling with no further billing regardless of the total effort
A guarantee that the final total will match the original estimate
Honest hours, surfaced changes, and a budget range with a checkpoint
A fixed price for each deliverable once the client scopes it out
questions.explanation: Because the client absorbs the overrun, the consultant owes transparency and a guardrail. Without a range and a checkpoint, an open-ended rate becomes a blank check.

questions.question: When a golden set case fails, what is the correct first response?
options: Rewrite the expected output to match what the system currently does so the gate turns green
Remove the failing case from the set so it stops blocking the planned release
Decide whether the system regressed or the world changed before touching it
Lower the pass bar slightly until the failing case passes again
questions.explanation: The set holds the quality bar, so a failure is a question to answer, not a bar to move. Moving the expected output to match the system deletes the record of what correct used to be.

questions.question: Which force most directly limits how fast discovery and design can move?
options: The number of tools and data sources the delivery touches
The model selected for each scheduled task
How fast the client's stakeholders respond
The size of the implementation backlog
questions.explanation: Stakeholders who must answer questions and approve scope control the pace, so review gates should be scheduled around their calendar, not the consultant's.

questions.question: When should the conversion gate be set?
options: After the pilot succeeds and the proof is clear
Only if the client later asks to pay for more
At the very end, during contract negotiation
Before the pilot starts, with terms sketched
questions.explanation: After the pilot succeeds the power shifts to the client, so the gate and its terms must be agreed before the proof exists.

questions.question: Why does agent security rely on defense in depth rather than one strong control?
options: Because a firewall placed at the network edge stops every realistic agent threat
Because the model's own safety training is sufficient to contain the agent
Because separate profiles sandbox the agent and fully contain its filesystem access
Because no single layer covers every boundary, so one catches what another misses
questions.explanation: Each layer covers a different boundary, so a gap in one is caught by another. A setup with one strong control and five gaps is a gate with an open field around it.

questions.question: When must the baseline for an outcome metric be captured, and why?
options: At the end of the engagement, drawn from the client's memory of the old process
Whenever it is convenient once the agent is already running in production
Before the solution exists, from the client's real data, agreed in writing
Only if the buyer later requests a formal before-and-after comparison
questions.explanation: A baseline reconstructed after delivery gets idealized in memory, which makes it contested. Freezing it in writing from real data before the solution exists keeps the comparison honest.

questions.question: When a plan is sized for a client build, how should review cycles be treated?
options: As a formality that costs almost no calendar time
As a single pass that runs only at the end
As a small step absorbed into the build effort
As a bottleneck to plan several cycles for
questions.explanation: The show, feedback, and revise loop eats real calendar time, so a plan should assume more than one review cycle rather than a single pass.

questions.question: What makes a skill's description effective for a reusable toolkit?
options: It summarizes the full text of the skill
It names the situation that triggers loading it
It lists every supporting file bundled inside the folder
It names the client the skill came from
questions.explanation: The description is the only thing the agent sees when deciding whether to load the skill, so it must name the situation, not the content.

questions.question: How do the operating doc and the runbook differ?
options: The operating doc is the recovery procedure for failures, and the runbook is the reference for how it is configured
The operating doc is calm reference for configuration, and the runbook is procedure for when it breaks
The operating doc is written for the client, and the runbook is written only for the original builder
The operating doc is written under pressure, and the runbook is written calmly beforehand
questions.explanation: The operating doc answers how the system is put together and configured, read calmly. The runbook answers what to do when something broke, written calmly but read in a hurry by a stranger.

questions.question: Which sequencing practice best reflects how the IT, compliance, and legal gates should be handled?
options: Finish building the agent first, then ask each team how long its review will take
Treat the three teams as one obstacle and clear them together at the very end
Start the slow gates in parallel with the build so the channel is open at go-live
Present one technical demonstration to all three teams in a single meeting
questions.explanation: The slowest gate is the schedule, so the sticky gates are started early and run beside the build. Planning backward from go-live keeps the channel open when the agent is ready.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an eval suite built from known-good cases?
options: To make every scheduled run finish more quickly
To remove the need for a human to review output
To catch silent regressions when inputs change
To record every command the agent issues in a log
questions.explanation: A fixed set of known-good cases with expected outputs catches the quiet degradation that a rule, data, or model change can introduce.

questions.question: How should a consultant handle the possibility that another initiative shares credit for an improvement?
options: Name it first and claim only the share the agent can honestly own
Leave it out of the report so the agent's contribution looks larger
Report only a metric for which no other initiative could apply
Wait for the buyer to raise it and then adjust the numbers afterward
questions.explanation: The buyer will think of the other initiative anyway, so naming it first and conceding its weight keeps the claim credible. Claiming only the provable share is what makes the report believed.

questions.question: Which four steps make up the change-order discipline for a request past the baseline?
options: Quote the work, negotiate the fee, absorb the difference, and reconcile at the end
Warn the client, log the request, delay the work, and revisit it monthly
Name the delta, name the trade, get a yes, and write it into the baseline
Decline the request, escalate to the sponsor, rebaseline, and restaff the work
questions.explanation: Every request is stated as a precise delta and paired with a visible trade in time, price, or scope. The client owns the trade and the change is recorded so the baseline stays the source of truth.

questions.question: A delivery stalls suddenly. Where is the failure most likely to live?
options: In a provider or infrastructure link, such as a timeout or an expired key
In the agent's orchestration logic, since that is the code you yourself wrote
In the client's expectations, which have drifted from the delivered scope
In the quality gate, which blocked the run before it could deliver anything
questions.explanation: An agent is a chain of orchestration, provider, tools, and environment, and a sudden stall usually sits in the provider or infrastructure link. Assuming the software is at fault wastes most incident time.

questions.question: What goes wrong when the payment schedule does not match the risk allocation priced into the engagement?
options: It becomes a second, conflicting agreement that overrides the risk allocation
It has no effect, because the pricing decision already governs the engagement
It automatically converts the engagement from fixed-fee to time-and-materials
It makes the statement of work unenforceable for both parties at once
questions.explanation: The payment terms are where the risk allocation becomes money changing hands. When they disagree with the pricing, the mismatch acts as a second contract that wins the argument.

questions.question: What are the three capabilities that make up ownership of a delivered system?
options: Reading, writing, and archiving the operating documentation
Running the system, changing it, and passing it to the next person
Monitoring, alerting, and escalating problems back to the consultant
Building, testing, and deploying new versions of the system
questions.explanation: Ownership is operational, change, and sustaining capability together, and each is taught differently. Training only the first leaves a team that is frozen or a single point of failure.

questions.question: Why is a specific scope boundary, paired with an out-of-scope list, central to protecting both sides?
options: It lets the client make additions without ever going through any process
It hides the parts of the engagement the seller remains unsure about
It gives a reference that classifies any request as in or out
It guarantees the project will finish ahead of the agreed schedule
questions.explanation: A boundary specific enough to classify any request is what lets a change be priced instead of argued. Naming what is excluded prevents the client from assuming it is included.

questions.question: Where should buffers be placed in an engagement plan, and why?
options: As one large cushion in the final week, so recovery is concentrated
Evenly across every week, so no single phase carries more risk
At the points of genuine uncertainty, such as after a technical spike and before handover
Only after the last gate, so the estimate stays a single clean number
questions.explanation: A single end-of-plan buffer moves all risk to the final week, where it cannot be recovered from. Small buffers positioned where uncertainty actually lives absorb surprises where they occur.

questions.question: What separates a composed set of scope, plan, and estimate artifacts from three documents that are merely stacked?
options: Each artifact is written in the same template and reviewed by the same person
Each artifact improves the other two, so deleting one would weaken the rest
Each artifact is delivered to the client on the same day
Each artifact repeats the others' content so the reader can cross-check them
questions.explanation: The composition test is interdependence: a scope that adds no gate to the plan, or a plan that prices nothing new, is just separate paperwork. Each artifact should strengthen the other two rather than sit beside them.

questions.question: When packaging an engagement into a reusable skill, what should you keep?
options: The client's names and specific data formats
The complete record of the original engagement
The transferable core, minus client detail
Only the parts that were difficult to build
questions.explanation: A reusable skill keeps the procedure that transfers and strips the client-specific detail, or the next engagement cannot put it to use.

questions.question: A tool has no primitive that carries an important intent. What should you do?
options: Improvise a fragile approximation and call the translation done
Force the tool to behave like the reference tool until it almost works
Name the capability gap with its price and the client's options
Copy the reference artifact into the tool's format and assume it holds
questions.explanation: An honest capability gap is itself a deliverable with a price and a sign-off. Papering it over leaves an intent that only looks enforced, which is worse than a reported limitation.

questions.question: What should the pilot's slice be?
options: The whole problem, so the client sees it work
The easiest part, so the pilot cannot fail
A representative slice on the real data
A synthetic sample chosen to flatter the tool
questions.explanation: The slice must be representative of real data and failure modes yet bounded, so it proves the mechanism without becoming the delivery.

questions.question: What makes an acceptance bar clause usable when the work is handed over?
options: A stranger with the test set could grade it without exercising judgment
It is written in the client's own words rather than the consultant's
It is agreed verbally with the sponsor before the build starts
It is restated in the estimate as a line item with a price
questions.explanation: An acceptance clause must be a testable claim: a person with no context and the test set can grade every clause. If a clause needs judgment to evaluate, it belongs in a risk note instead.

questions.question: What does a sandboxed deploy actually guarantee about the agent's behavior?
options: It automatically approves every dangerous command in a run
It removes the need for any guardrails
It grants the agent write access to production
It isolates where the agent runs, not what it does
questions.explanation: Isolation and approval are separate layers: the sandbox controls where the agent runs, and the guardrail set still controls what it may do there.

questions.question: In a complex client environment, what is the right starting move?
options: Design the ideal system, then adapt the environment to it
Map the existing environment, then design to fit it
Replace the old stack with a cleaner one
Ignore constraints until deployment time
questions.explanation: The environment is given and will reject a design that ignores it, so mapping the stack and its constraints comes before designing the delivery.

questions.question: What turns a sequence of phases into a repeatable, priceable delivery framework?
options: Defined outputs and gates before work moves to the next phase
A detailed timeline that lists every task in chronological order
A flexible plan the consultant reinvents for each new client engagement
A fixed method that is never revised once it has been written down
questions.explanation: Gates are where variation gets caught early and where a failure becomes cheap and visible. A known process with known outputs is estimable and priceable in a way an improvisation is not.

questions.question: Where should redundancy be placed in an agent estate?
options: On every job equally, so that no single run in the estate can ever miss
On the cheapest and most frequent jobs, since those fire the greatest number of times
On the inference path, and only where the cost of a missed run is high
On the data sources, since those are the widest dependency the fleet shares
questions.explanation: The one truly shared component is the inference path, so redundancy belongs there. Redundancy is insurance priced against the cost of a lost run, spent only where failure is expensive.

questions.question: Why should an agent pipeline validate its input shape and stop rather than continue when the input changes?
options: Because stopping reduces the number of model tokens each run consumes
Because a loud failure is cheaper to diagnose than quiet wrong output
Because validation removes the need for any human to review the output
Because source schemas are guaranteed never to change again once matched
questions.explanation: The tempting failure mode keeps producing output that looks fine, which is worse than stopping. Designing for a loud, dated failure makes the problem cheap and visible instead of shipping wrong drafts.

questions.question: Why should acceptance criteria be written as tests rather than as descriptions?
options: They make the document look more rigorous to the client's legal team
They let both sides know what done means and can be run and counted
They let the seller state the price before the client agrees to any scope
They remove the need for an out-of-scope list in the contract
questions.explanation: A description such as accurate enforces nothing, while a test with a pass bar can be run and counted. Testable criteria turn done from an argument into a fact.

questions.question: Why must a quality system at scale run both a gate and a sample?
options: A gate catches regressions caused by a change, while a sample catches drift
A gate catches drift over time, while a sample catches change-driven regressions
A gate replaces the golden set, while a sample replaces the need for a gate
A gate screens each live output, while a sample audits the golden set's cases
questions.explanation: A change-triggered gate and a human sample of the live stream cover opposite failures: what a change broke and what drifted with no change at all. Running only one leaves half the estate unverified.

questions.question: How should credentials appear in the operating doc?
options: As their actual values, so that the operator can confirm each one directly
As their existence, location, and owner, never their value
Omitted entirely from the doc, so that nothing sensitive is ever written down
As an encrypted block that the operator decrypts whenever it is needed
questions.explanation: The doc records what exists and where it lives so the operator knows what to refresh and whom to ask. Writing the value in turns a configuration note into a breach.

questions.question: When translating the same technical decision to the legal team, what should the consultant present?
options: A liability-bounded scope stating what the agent will not do
A feature demonstration that shows how capable the agent is
An audit trail and retention record that shows what the data does
A deployment plan describing where it runs and how it authenticates
questions.explanation: Legal limits the organization's exposure, so it needs the scope written as a bound on liability. A deployment plan serves IT and audit evidence serves compliance.

questions.question: What is the main problem with running every task on one model?
options: It makes the provider and env configuration harder to manage
It overpays easy work and underperforms hard work
It caps the number of scheduled jobs the agent can run
It forces every task onto the cheapest available model
questions.explanation: A single default treats trivial and demanding work as equal, so the easy task overpays and the hard task runs on a model too weak for it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the weekly portfolio review?
options: To measure each client's profit margin against the margins of all the others
To renegotiate every client's contract at the start of each week
To force the whole set into view so a quiet client does not quietly starve
To replace the need for any written scope agreement with any of the clients
questions.explanation: The engagement in front of you always demands attention, and the client you are not looking at is the one that starves. A fixed review forces the whole portfolio into view on a cadence.

questions.question: How should the ongoing operation of an agent be priced?
options: As part of the one-time build total
As a per-run cost only, with no ongoing rate
As a weekly rate kept apart from the build
As a fixed fee paid once at handover
questions.explanation: The build is a one-time total while the ongoing operation recurs weekly, so it is priced as a rate plus a per-run cost.

questions.question: How should the price of a recurring agent operation be determined?
options: From the real per-run cost of the pinned model and provider, plus margin
From the market rate other vendors charge for similar agent work
From the buyer's stated budget spread across the length of the engagement
From the number of sessions the agent happened to run during the pilot
questions.explanation: The price is a claim about your unit economy, so it is built from the actual cost of the pinned configuration with margin. Numbers read from the run record beat a market guess.

questions.question: Against what should the value of a delivered engagement be measured at the close?
options: Against a definition agreed before the change, reported honestly
Against the final state of the system the agent happens to have produced
Against the vendor's own dashboard activity metrics for the run period
Against whichever improvement looks strongest in the final week of the engagement
questions.explanation: Measurement needs a definition that predates the change, so the agreed metric is the one reported. Reporting the smaller, verifiable number builds a claim the buyer can check and trust.

questions.question: A requirement captures the process as-built when it records which version?
options: The process as written in the official documentation
The process as actually performed in practice
The process the sponsor describes in a meeting
The process the vendor's manual prescribes
questions.explanation: The as-built view is the process as performed, which is what the build must match, because the documented version diverges and breaks on real data.

questions.question: Under a fixed-fee contract, who carries the estimation risk, and when is the mechanism the right choice?
options: The client carries it, because the price is fixed and known in advance
You carry it, and it fits work whose scope you genuinely know
Neither party carries it, because the price is agreed before work begins
You carry it, and it fits exploratory work you cannot yet scope
questions.explanation: Fixed-fee loads the overrun risk onto the consultant, which is fair only when the work is understood well enough to price. Exploratory work belongs under a rate instead.

questions.question: What number defines the estimate for a multi-week delivery?
options: The sum of all task effort across the plan
The longest chain of dependent work
The average of the three-point ranges
The total number of scoped tasks
questions.explanation: The end date is set by the longest chain of dependent work, because parallel workstreams run at the same time rather than one after another.

questions.question: Which responsibility belongs to compliance rather than to IT or legal during an agent rollout?
options: Provisioning the environment and approving when production changes are allowed
Maintaining the standards the organization has committed to, such as audit
Bounding the organization's liability through the contracts that it signs
Writing the marketing plan that sells the agent to the client's staff
questions.explanation: Compliance owns the rules the organization has committed to and is satisfiable by evidence, not enthusiasm. IT controls the environment and legal controls the contractual frame.

questions.question: How do you know a translation actually worked?
options: When every file has been placed correctly in the new tool's expected format
When the intent's bad outcome is still prevented under real use
When the new tool's syntax matches the reference tool's syntax exactly
When the client signs off that the whole migration is complete and closed
questions.explanation: The test is behavior, not artifact: the bad outcome the intent exists to prevent must still be prevented. Files landing in the right place proves nothing about whether the discipline held.

questions.question: What is a delivery lead's own deliverable?
options: The most difficult piece of the production work
A personal sign-off on every finished task
A weekly status update for the client
The team's shape and the integrity of its seams
questions.explanation: A lead decomposes, routes, and watches the seams, and steps out of execution so the seams get the attention the team depends on.

questions.question: When an unattended run meets a dangerous command and no one is present to approve it, what is the safe default?
options: Approve it automatically so the run completes
Skip the check and log a warning instead
Retry the command on a stronger model
Deny it so the run stops or diverts
questions.explanation: A headless run should fail closed: blocking the command is the safe default, while auto-approval is reserved for a fully trusted, isolated environment.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a threat model?
options: The project budget, the delivery schedule, and the written acceptance criteria
The assets, the actors who threaten them, and the trust boundaries
The model, the provider, and the terminal backend in use
The scope, the identified risks, and the rollback plan
questions.explanation: A threat model names what you are protecting, who threatens it, and the lines an actor must cross to reach it. Without that structure every security decision is a guess on the client's behalf.

questions.question: A change to a job that runs unattended needs what?
options: No gate at all, since no person is present to notice a failure
A gate or check that runs after the change, because no person is watching
A larger scope that bundles in any other tidy-ups while you are already there
A blanket approval mode shared with interactive, human-driven work
questions.explanation: When nothing human is in the loop, the only thing that notices a bad change is an automated guard or eval. What separates a safe change from a dangerous one is often whether anything is watching after it lands.
